A strait reopening on Tehran's coordinates. 78,000 people across a border on the wrong continent. An outbreak travelling by river.

Five stories from this week where the real subject was geography.

5 ways the map moved — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Iran says its talks with Oman on the Strait of Hormuz are in their final stages — an understanding reached on the coordinates of a shipping route (BBC, Guardian).

NYT: agreeing a route would effectively ratify Tehran's control of it.

33 km wide at the narrowest.

2/ Ceuta's mayor-president says 78,000 crossed from Morocco and 100 died; up to 5,000 remain in the city (BBC, Guardian).

The Guardian asks whether Rabat feels emboldened by its closeness to Washington.

Ceuta and Moroccan Fnideq stand about a mile apart (NYT).

3/ Israel struck southern Lebanon after accusing Hezbollah of breaking the ceasefire — while negotiators met in Rome (NYT). Residents report fresh displacement orders (Al Jazeera).

The UN drew the Blue Line in 2000 as a withdrawal line. It was never agreed as a border.

4/ Ukraine hit two oil refineries deep inside Russia to cut war revenues (BBC). Russian drones have struck hundreds of Ukrainian filling stations in reply (NYT).

Odesa's docks are wrecked; a missile attack on Kyiv killed 17.

The front barely moved. The energy map did.

5/ Ebola cases in DR Congo have passed 4,000 and the virus may be mutating (Guardian). Africa CDC will deploy a vaccine made for a different strain; WHO says cases doubled in some hotspots in a week (DW).

A river boat is under quarantine after five deaths (BBC).

The historical parallel: European colonies in Africa, 1880 vs 1913.

Read it for what didn't change. Spain's two specks opposite Gibraltar sit in both panels — and outlived the protectorate that later surrounded them.

Ceuta: Portuguese 1415, Spanish 1668. Still there.
